---
title: "Object-words and abstract-words leave different marks in language models"
subtitle: "Florin Cojocariu · November 2026"
toc: true
---

Take the word "cat". You can use it of the cat on your lap, or of cats in general: "Cats hunt at night." Same word, different use. The experiment reported here asks whether that difference leaves a trace in a language model, a system that has only ever seen text.

It does. Where the model places a word depends on which way the word is being used, and the trace is the same from word to word: a rule learned from sentences about ten nouns sorts sentences about ten other nouns it has never seen. It is not genre, not grammar, and not the concreteness of the surrounding words. It is also thin: present, but not one of the main things that vary when a word changes sentence.

The rest of this page says why that is worth knowing and how to read the result pages.

## The result in one picture

Each dot is one sentence containing "dog", "fork", "tomato" or one of seven other nouns. Its position comes from a simple rule, a single straight cut through the model's representations, worked out only from sentences about ten *different* nouns ("cat", "hammer", "apple" and others). Sentences about one particular thing (dark blue) land on the left; general statements (orange) land on the right; idioms (grey) fall in between. The rule never saw these ten words and still sorts them.

## The distinction being tested

Take two sentences with the same word: "The cat jumped off the table and knocked the cup over" and "Cats hunt at night." The first is about one cat on one occasion. It reports an encounter, and it could be true of exactly one animal on one afternoon. The second is about no cat. It holds of the kind, it can be said in a room with no cat in it, and no particular cat makes it true.

The Pattern Constellations Framework (PCF) treats this as a difference between two modes of a word. In object-mode, written $x^{o}$, the word is used in the presence of an instance. In a child, $x^{o}$ forms as a motor pattern inside the pattern-constellation \{X\} that the encounters with the thing have built. It belongs to pre-verbal experience, and it is used only while that experience is active. In abstract-mode, written $x^{a}$, the word runs detached from any instance: in general statements, in idioms, in definitions. A word can have only this mode. "Electron" is learned from its meaning alone, with no encounter and no $electron^{o}$. Earlier write-ups called this mode $x^{c}$; the new name records that detachment from the centre is detachment from a history, and that is what abstraction is.

The two modes meet in the concept, which PCF writes $\mathcal{R}(x^{o}, x^{a})$: the word I use for what I experienced as x, linked to all the ways I can use the word x in language. The same linking relation writes the two kinds of sentence above. "This cat jumped" is $\mathcal{R}(cat^{o}, jump^{a})$. "Cats hunt" is $\mathcal{R}(cat^{a}, hunt^{a})$.

## Why look for it in a language model

Meaning lives in language. Each speaker has a personal linguistic pattern-constellation ⟨x⟩, shaped by a history of use. Public use of a word, $\overline{\langle x \rangle}$, is the aggregate of all uses as they lie in the sediment of written text. No living person holds it. A large language model is the one thing that comes close, because its training compresses that sediment.

The encounter is not in the sediment. A sentence written from an encounter does not carry the cat, the afternoon, or the writer's concern. What it can carry is the way people write when they write from an encounter: what they attend to, what they predicate, how they situate the thing in time. If that way of writing is regular enough across writers and words, training will have picked it up, and the model will embed $x^{o}$ uses and $x^{a}$ uses of a word in different places.

So the experiment asks a narrow question: does the text sediment carry a mark of the mode of use, and has the model extracted it as one feature shared across words?

## What an answer would show

A positive answer does two things.

It gives the $x^{o}$/$x^{a}$ distinction a foothold outside PCF's notation. The distinction was introduced to describe what happens in a person. If it also shows up as a regularity in public text, found by a model that knows nothing of the framework, then it is a real division in how language is used, and the notation tracks it.

It also says what the model has. The model has the mark of object-mode and none of what makes it object-mode. No encounter stands behind any of its sentences. Its "rod", the region where object-mode uses gather, is a substitute for $x^{o}$ built from sediment, which is the reading of LLMs the framework already gives: a renderer of $\overline{\langle x \rangle}$, restricted by the prompt, with no centre and no history behind the rendering.

A negative answer would also be informative. It would mean that writing from an encounter leaves no regular trace in text, and that the difference between the modes lives only in the speakers. PCF does not need the trace to exist. The claim that LLMs build a substitute for $x^{o}$ from the sediment would fall.

The results are evidence for the distinction and are not the distinction. Geometry in an embedding space is a picture of sediment. It is never the practice that left the sediment, and the pages that follow should not be read as showing that a model has object-mode, understands, or refers.

## Where this comes from

The experiment rewrites a study from 2025, "Patterns, Instrumentalism, and Mild Realism". That study sorted sentences into literal and figurative uses of words like "cat" and "fork", embedded them with SBERT, and found literal uses clustering tightly ("rods") and figurative uses spreading wide ("caps"). It read the rod as the object-word and the cap as the word-concept.

Two things went wrong. First, the validation was circular: the literal and figurative categories were cut from the same projection that was then used to validate the axis. Corrected with held-out data, external labels and transfer to other words, the separation survived, weaker (AUC 0.925 on external validation, 0.760 to 0.990 across words). Second, and more important, the cut was the wrong one. "Cats are mammals" is literal and abstract-mode. "Let the cat out of the bag" is figurative and also abstract-mode. Literal and figurative is a division inside $x^{a}$, and comparing it with object-mode mixed two differences. It also let a confound in: figurative uses of a word come from many unrelated topics, so they spread for that reason alone.

The new experiment keeps the question and changes the cut. Object-mode is compared with literal general predication, $\mathcal{R}(cat^{o}, p)$ against $\mathcal{R}(cat^{a}, p)$, so that literalness is held fixed and only the mode varies. Idioms and definitions are kept as separate groups and never pooled.

## How the experiment is built

The sentences are natural, taken from encyclopedic text and from fiction, for twenty concrete nouns split into two halves. Every choice of method is made on the first half. The second half is used once, at the end.

::: {.proposed-edit}
No sentence is labeled by a person. Every sentence is labeled by a language model that reads only the labeling criterion. A sample of 300 sentences is labeled a second time, separately, and every result is also reported on that sample alone. A local model from a different family relabels everything as a cross-check.
[Proposed change. Original: "A sample of 300 sentences is labeled by hand, and every result is also reported on that sample alone."]{.was}
:::

from _site import stage_flow
stage_flow()

The results answer four questions in turn. Each test is one experiment, E1 to E8; the numbers are the ids used in the summary and the data files, not the order of the argument.

**Is there a mark?**

- **Shared direction (E2).** Does a probe trained on some words separate the modes in words it never saw? If each word only had its own two clusters, it would not.

**Is it something else?**

- **Not genre (E3).** Does the direction carry over from encyclopedic text to fiction and back? Encyclopedias are mostly abstract-mode and novels mostly object-mode, so a genre detector would fail here.
- **Not grammar (E4).** Does the direction do better than a classifier that sees only determiners, number and tense, and does it survive pairs of sentences with the same surface form ("The cat is on the mat" and "The cat is a solitary hunter")?
- **Not concreteness (E5).** Does it survive when the concreteness of the other words in the sentence is removed?

**Does it behave as a mark of the mode should?**

- **Agreement across models (E7).** Do an encoder, a decoder and a sentence model order the same sentences in the same way?
- **Predictions (E6).** Definitions are meaning with no occasion at all, so they should sit at the far abstract end of a direction that never saw them. Where idioms fall is an open question.

**How visible is it without labels?**

- **Prominence (E1).** Is the mode one of the main directions along which a word's embeddings vary, with nothing telling the model or the analysis what to look for? This is the test that would support "extracted from the sediment" most directly. It is also the most demanding: a mark can be real, shared and thin. It comes last because it describes the mark the other tests establish.

**Beyond English**

- **Not English syntax (E8)** (if Romanian data is supplied). Does the direction learned on English carry over to Romanian, which marks definiteness differently?

## How to read the results

::: {.proposed-edit}
The result pages follow the four questions in that order. Each states the question, the numbers on the full set and on the separately labeled sample, and a verdict per model. A closing section lists every test that did not hold outright or had too little data to decide. The claim stands as far as the tests hold and no further. If the probe does not beat the grammar classifier, the mark is carried mainly by grammar, and the paper becomes a paper about how grammar records the mode.
